title: Yalumba unveils the 2026 Rare & Fine Collection
summary:
Yalumba, Australia’s oldest family-owned winery, is set to launch its 2026 Rare & Fine Collection, with the flagship Signature Cabernet Sauvignon, Shiraz 2023 available exclusively through online retailer The Wine Society exclusively from the middle of this month (19 August).

The post Yalumba unveils the 2026 Rare & Fine Collection appeared first on The Drinks Business.
content: Yalumba, Australia’s oldest family-owned winery, is set to launch its 2026 Rare & Fine Collection, with the flagship Signature Cabernet Sauvignon, Shiraz 2023 available exclusively through online retailer The Wine Society exclusively from the middle of this month (19 August). The 2026 release comprises six wines from four recent vintages (2021 to 2024), which use grapes some of the estate’s best vines and includes blends from across Barossa and Coonawarra. It includes The Caley Cabernet Sauvignon, Shiraz 2021, The Octavius Old Vine Shiraz 2021, The Tri-Centenary Grenache 2024, The Menzies Cabernet Sauvignon 2022 and The Steeple Shiraz 2022.  In additions, the Signature Cabernet Sauvignon, Shiraz 2023 will be released as part of The Wine Society's in-bond First Release programme (in bond), which a spokesman from the Wine Society called "an absolute bargain". Sam Wigan, head winemaker at Yalumba said it was “not a given” that the estate makes each Rare & Fine wine every year, preferring to do so “only when all elements of viticulture and winemaking align to deliver something special.” He called the 2026 Collection “an outstanding example of Yalumba’s regional and varietal expertise, and a true testament to the Hill-Smith family’s fine wine legacy.” “Each of the collection’s six wines reflect the individuality of our old and cherished vines and the precision of our winemaking. Together, they embody our long-term vision, highlighting our dedication to diversity and authenticity in fine wine,” he said. He explained that the span of four vintages was “the hallmark of Yalumba’s regional expertise and fine wine philosophy”, noting that the Grenache “shines in its youth”, while the Cabernet and Shiraz blends “benefit from time in bottle.” “Our annual Rare & Fine collection is designed to reflect the rhythm of our vineyards and the diversity of our craft.” Fifth-generation owner Robert Hill-Smith added that the Rare & Fine collection wines “remind us that legacy is written one season at a time”. “Each vintage captures our heritage and our responsibility to the future, crafting wines that endure, from vines that have endured.”

title: Fine wine businesses ‘have to plan for a leaner, more efficient world’
summary:
With fine wine potentially entering a period of “profound structural change”, with industry consolidation “inevitable”, businesses “have to plan for a leaner, more efficient world”, according to Jeremy Howard, CEO of Cru World Wine.

The post Fine wine businesses ‘have to plan for a leaner, more efficient world’ appeared first on The Drinks Business.
content:
With fine wine potentially entering a period of “profound structural change” with industry consolidation “inevitable”, businesses “have to plan for a leaner, more efficient world”, according to Jeremy Howard, CEO of Cru World Wine. Howard pointed out that there were “too many sub-scale merchants and fragmented inventory holders… within the distribution chain”, which created duplicated costs and “unnecessary friction.” Previously the temporary surge in demand during Covid had “masked these inefficiencies”, he said, but that was no longer the case.

Leaner and meaner

He pointed to some analysis he had conducted indicated that “the top 15 UK fine wine companies are losing nearly £20 million a year at the moment - and it's not sustainable.” “They're eating their balance sheets,” he argued, pointing out that “they need a more efficient way of operating” by becoming “leaner and meaner on the inside”. “There are lots of reasons to be cautious about top line [stats] as the top 15 UK fine wine companies are still selling almost £850 million pounds a year in wine. And if you multiply this around the world, that is a lot of fine wine being bought. But the problem is, they're spending £210 million pounds a year in admin expenses to sell £850 million pounds of wine, and the margins just aren't there to support it.” He argued that there was “some denial out there” and many people were “holding out for the market to bounce back”. “If it happens, it will be great… but it feels to me that the boom in fine wine feels like a generational thing for a certain generation,” he said. Even if millennials and Gen Z drink more than many  headlines allow, “I'm not sure they're going to build 3,000 - 4,000 case wine collections in a way that I did and people I know did.” “I think we have to plan for a sort of a leaner world, more efficient world.”

Resilience

Speaking to db back in the Spring, Brett Fleming of Armit Wines had said that while he wanted to be optimistic, the headwinds of Trump and Putin’s wars increasing inflation as well as the UK’s current fiscal policy (“we have a government that doesn’t understand business,” he said of the then Starmer administration) meant businesses have to be resilient. “You have to be more resilient, you have to be adaptable, you have to take opportunities, and you’ve got to be able to absorb challenges. And sadly, other companies won't," he said. At the time, he argued that the consolidation was likely to both continue and “be more aggressive as it continues”, not just for distribution, but also in the on trade. He pointed to  Heston Blumenthal’s decision to close his two-starred Michelin restaurant ‘Dinner by Heston’ in the Mandarin Oriental at the end of January 2027, as an example. “I think they're going to see more of that, and that then just adds further pressure to the supply chain, because you've got fewer outlets of prestige, iconic status, being trying to be supplied by the same number of distributors. And lot of this can trace back to government fiscal policy.” Helen Miller, commercial director of Goedhuis Waddesdon (which was the product of two businesses coming together itself) agreed that the industry has to work together to survive the current challenges. She argued that the economics of business “had to make sense” and businesses are struggling. “I think when you can share - as we have with the infrastructure - and share the risk, I do think it [consolidation] makes sense.” “I would imagine that's something that we're going to see more [of],” she concluded. According to Howard, there is “just so much duplication” across the industry. “Every little company has to have somebody doing inventory management and somebody doing marketing and somebody doing finance and somebody placing purchase orders and somebody managing tech.” “Unfortunately, we are going to have to see some reductions in admin expenses in the industry, which is going to be unfortunate for some people, I fear. But I just I don't see what the alternative is.”

Technology

Technology in particular can prove “terribly difficult for smaller companies to keep up”, he argued. “The likely outcome is a market increasingly centred on one neutral, technology-driven marketplace owned by the participants who create its value. Ownership will extend beyond private collectors to include producers, merchants and major stockholders, all of whom stand to benefit from a more efficient and transparent marketplace.” This is the opportunity he sees for Cru World Wine to become the Rightmove of wine – “if we can provide a platform for them to operate, but to take away some of the costs that they currently all have to have in-house, then we might be able to have a situation where most of the companies survive, but under the hood, they're much smaller, and they don't have to have the same overheads.”

title: Bordeaux revives ‘Claret’ for new generation of drinkers
summary:
Bordeaux is revamping ‘claret’ for a modern wine-drinking audience, with an emphasis on light, low-tannin and unoaked wines destined for the fridge. Patrick Schmitt MW considers the facts.

The post Bordeaux revives ‘Claret’ for new generation of drinkers appeared first on The Drinks Business.
content:
Bordeaux is revamping ‘claret’ for a modern wine-drinking audience, with an emphasis on light, low-tannin and unoaked wines destined for the fridge. Patrick Schmitt MW considers the facts.

The world’s most famous wine region, and the benchmark for high-end Cabernets and Merlots, Bordeaux is reviving its historic ‘claret’ name as the banner for a new category of light, fruit-forward, chillable dry red wines aimed at attracting younger consumers back to region. The initiative, led by the Syndicat des AOC Bordeaux et Bordeaux Supérieur, follows a 2023 consultation prompted by falling red wine consumption and an ageing consumer base. Managing director of the Bordeaux et Bordeaux Supérieur Wine Union Stéphanie Sinoquet told the drinks business that the decision was informed by consumer research and product testing across six priority markets: the UK, France, Belgium, Germany, China and Japan. Rather than creating a new appellation, the union has introduced a regulated ‘mention traditionnelle’ called Bordeaux Claret, effective from the 2025 vintage. All Bordeaux red grape varieties are permitted, although early production has relied mainly on Merlot with some Malbec. Short maceration of two to four days produces lightly coloured, low-tannin, unoaked wines intended to be served chilled.

Begins where dark rosé ends

The specification defines Claret as a ruby to light-purple, fruit-forward red with moderate intensity, ripe red fruit aromas and a structure designed for early drinking. It begins where the dark rosé ‘Bordeaux Clairet’ ends, with a minimum Colour Intensity Index (ICM) of 3, while featuring less pronounced amylic character (such as cotton candy aromatics) than you might find in Clairet. Winemaking methods remain flexible, but every wine must meet the required sensory profile through assessment by an independent tasting panel. Minimum alcohol is set at 11% ABV, with most wines expected at 12%–13%. Malolactic fermentation is optional, and, while residual sugar is capped at 3g/l for the traditional style of Bordeaux, the cap is raised to 7g/l for the chillable expression. A minimum grape sugar level of 189g/l at harvest is also required to ensure sufficient fruit ripeness. De-alcoholisation is not permitted under PDO rules. chillable red It is recommended that producers display ‘Bordeaux Claret’ prominently on front labels, alongside descriptors such as ‘fruity’, ‘fresh’ or ‘chillable red’ to distinguish the style from traditional claret. Wines failing to meet the specification cannot use the designation.

Big Bordeaux brands on board

The first vintage has already exceeded expectations, with around 16,500 hectolitres – roughly two million bottles – produced by about 40 wineries. Importantly, participation extends beyond small estates to major négociants and brands including Calvet and Mouton Cadet. The marketing strategy is focused firmly on the on-trade, with by-the-glass service, including over ice, seen as the best way to build consumer awareness. Recommended serving temperature is around 5°C, although the wines are intended to perform well up to 10°C–12°C. Promotional activity will initially target France, Belgium, Germany and the UK through trade events and media, rather than consumer advertising. In the UK specifically, a small group of buyers for London merchants are reluctant to lose the term ‘claret’ for traditional red Bordeaux, encouraging the wine growers union to emphasise the broader “chillable red” category in its messaging. Outside the UK, claret doesn’t carry the same fame and association. The relaunch has prompted discussion within Bordeaux over whether the claret designation should eventually be shared more widely across France, although any change would require a formal vote. The launch comes as Bordeaux continues to contract its vineyard area following years of oversupply. Regional vineyard area has fallen sharply since 2021 through uprooting and reclassification, providing the backdrop against which Bordeaux Claret’s commercial performance will be judged.

The background

  • 'Claret' is not a new invention: it was the name given by English merchants to the lighter-coloured Bordeaux wines exported after the marriage of Eleanor of Aquitaine and Henry II in 1152.
  • While 'claret' became the generic British term for Bordeaux red, Bordeaux is now reclaiming the word to define a specific modern wine style.

The launch

  • Bordeaux Claret is a new regulated category introduced under the Bordeaux AOC as a mention traditionnelle (traditional designation), rather than a new appellation. It applies from the 2025 vintage.
  • The initiative was officially unveiled at Wine Paris 2026 after a fast-tracked approval process with France's wine regulator, the INAO.

The wine style

  • Light-coloured ruby red
  • Fruit-driven with soft tannins
  • Unoaked
  • Intended to be served chilled
  • Designed for early drinking rather than cellaring
  • Sits stylistically between traditional Bordeaux red and Bordeaux Clairet

Production rules

  • All Bordeaux red varieties are permitted
  • Merlot is expected to dominate early releases
  • Short maceration produces lower colour and tannin
  • Wines must pass an independent tasting panel
  • Minimum 11% ABV
  • Residual sugar up to 7g/l
  • De-alcoholisation is prohibited

Commercial rollout

  • Around 40 producers have already made Bordeaux Claret
  • The first vintage totals roughly 16,500hl (around two million bottles)
  • Participants include major brands such as Mouton Cadet and Calvet, suggesting broad industry backing rather than a niche experiment

Marketing strategy

  • Focus is on restaurants and bars rather than retail
  • Promotion centres on by-the-glass service
  • Wines are recommended served around 5°C (and remain suitable up to 10-12°C)
  • Marketing emphasises descriptors such as "fresh", "fruity" and "chillable red"

title: Bibi Graetz reflects on leaving La Place de Bordeaux
summary:
On a recent visit to Tuscany, db's Bordeaux correspondent, Colin Hay talked to Bibi Graetz about his decision to leave La place de Bordeaux and his ambition, which has always been "to make better and better wines". 

The post Bibi Graetz reflects on leaving La Place de Bordeaux appeared first on The Drinks Business.
content: On a recent visit to Tuscany, db's Bordeaux correspondent, Colin Hay talked to Bibi Graetz about his decision to leave La place de Bordeaux and his ambition, which has always been "to make better and better wines".  It is hardly a jealously guarded secret that the world of fine wine is today in crisis. And crisis is an accelerator of change. One symptom of that change is the rapid evolution of La Place de Bordeaux, notably with respect to its offering of wines from beyond Bordeaux itself. I took the opportunity of a recent trip to Florence to visit one of La Place’s most iconic of ‘hors Bordeaux’ stars, Bibi Graetz. From his tasting room perch in Fiesole, overlooking the city below, we talked about his almost immediate success on La Place de Bordeaux and his painful and difficult decision to leave it last year. Below is a simple précis of our conversation. Given the sensitivity and importance of many of the issues we discussed I offer no analysis here of the implications of his comments (that is for later) and I prefer to leave Bibi’s thoughts in his own words. But I would like to record my extreme gratitude to him for sharing with us his reflections on what is undoubtedly a painful episode with much wider implications for La Place and the world of fine wine today. Describe to us your history with La Place. How did it all begin?  I had been thinking at La Place already for many years but couldn’t find an entry route. Suddenly, in 2018, I found an open window and I jumped. I met a négociant at the first Tuscany en primeur tasting of James Suckling, and we became partners and good friends. What made this such a success from the start? I was super creative and was coming with new and fresh ideas all the time. And very fast, it became a huge success, probably one of the greatest ‘beyond Bordeaux’ success stories. In three years, the brand exploded, and we established Testamatta and Colore on the global fine wine scene. These wines attained a whole new level of worldwide recognition which we are very proud of still today. It has been so much fun, and everybody was a bit ‘drunk’ from this incredible success; we really loved it all. So what went wrong?  In 2023 something changed. I came in Bordeaux in August, just before the September release, and one of my closest négociant friends told me: ‘Bibi the situation is dramatic!’. He said: ‘the only phrase I have to describe it is … FASTEN YOUR SEAT BELTS, this is going to be difficult …. And what we are seeing now is not the bottom, it is only going to get worse!’. Things has already started slowing down and by the time we arrived at the release of the 2023 vintage in September 2025 the négociants were under financial pressure. They wanted to act as agents and not as négociants anymore, buying only what, in effect, they had already sold. The result was that they could not commit to the vintage, or at least not for the ‘beyond Bordeaux’ wines like ours. We told them that without commitment we would leave … The rest, as they say, is history!  The reaction from our partners was really fast. They took the opportunity, stepped back in and committed where the négociants of La Place would not.  How does that decision feel today? And what does the future hold for you? With La Place de Bordeaux, we reached heights that I had never thought possible in my wildest dreams. So we are sorry that we were obliged to leave. But, on the other hand, we are thankful for the opportunity, all we did together and for what we achieved with La Place. Now our focus is on maintaining what we have built. We believe that nowadays exclusive distribution is the best way to go. We have a very strong brand and that is a blessing in today’s complicated global market situation. Our drive has always been to make better and better wines. Consistent with that, from the 2022 vintage onwards, all our wine will come from vineyards above 400 metres. That reduces significantly our overall production whilst bringing a whole new dimension to our wines, with incredible parfums, freshness and acidity.

title: Australians brace for alcohol tax hike blow
summary:
From Monday, tax on RTDs and spirits is set to leap to AU$110.15 per litre in Australia in what is one of the largest six-month increases outside of Covid. 

The post Australians brace for alcohol tax hike blow appeared first on The Drinks Business.
content:
From Monday, tax on RTDs and spirits is set to leap to AU$110.15 per litre in Australia in what is one of the largest six-month increases outside of Covid.  Australians are bracing to pay more for spirits and packaged beer, as the Australian federal government imposes its 79th alcohol tax hike in 40 years.  Australian brewers and distillers now pay the third highest tax rate in the world – only surpassed by several countries in Scandinavia – with the government preparing to cash in AU$9.1bn in total alcohol taxes this year. For a standard 700ml bottle of spirits, approximately $30 of the retail price is alcohol excise before GST is applied.  The twice-yearly automatic indexation was introduced by the Hawke Government in 1983, led by treasurer at the time Paul Keating.  But experts warn that the system is now encouraging a surge in demand for cheap, bootleg alcohol alternatives This follows research showing taxed spirits are becoming unaffordable, leading to soaring drink costs and demand for cheap, bootleg alternatives, with illicit alcohol now making up a 7.5% slice of total Australian alcohol by volume, with this figure even higher for bottled spirits.

'Driving demand'  for illicit alcohol

Steven Fanner, who became executive director of Spirits & Cocktails Australia last year, said: “We have a system where twice-yearly tax hikes on alcohol have been on auto-pilot since the early 1980s. “This means that from next week the tax on spirits is now over $110 per litre of pure alcohol – a rate six times higher than the United States and about double New Zealand. “This is not a system that should be a set-and-forget — without reform the government risks a myriad of unintended consequences, including driving demand for cheap, black-market alternatives.” However, others have embraced the hikes. Speaking to 7News, Nicole Lee, CEO of Hello Sunday Morning, said: “There’s absolutely no doubt that increasing the excise helps reduce public health problems.”

Draught beer and wine dodge the hike

Draught beer is exempt from the biannual hikes, as part of the two-year tax holiday that commenced in August 2025.  When it first came into force, the draught beer tax freeze marked the first time either the spirits or beer tax remained level since automatic indexation was introduced. Since then the spirits sector has called for an extension to include draught spirits, but this was vetoed by the Senate.  Wine, too, is not impacted by the hikes, as it is subject to a separate tax system.

title: Draught beer is about to get more expensive in South Korea – here’s why
summary:
From the end of this year, South Korea will slash the 20% tax break on draught beer, the government has announced in the 2026 tax reform plan, with bars across the country bracing for cost increases. 

The post Draught beer is about to get more expensive in South Korea – here’s why appeared first on The Drinks Business.
content:
From the end of this year, South Korea will slash the 20% tax break on draught beer, the government has announced in the 2026 tax reform plan, with bars across the country bracing for cost increases.  Bars and restaurants across South Korea are steeling themselves  for price hikes after the government announced that the 20% tax holiday on draught beer will end from next year, according to the Ministry of Finance and Economy’s 2026 tax reform package.  Currently, beer taxes are decided on volume instead of price. While standard beer is taxed at 885,700 won per kilolitre, the tax rate for draught beer is 708,560 – thanks to the 20% discount the category has been subject to since 2020. Six years ago, the government issued the 20% tax holiday in a bid to help the draught beer industry, whose tax burden had grown disproportionately large, and the application period has since been extended multiple times. However, officials have now decided that the beer sector has sufficiently benefited from the reduction, prompting the decision to end it later this year. From 2027, the tax burden per glass is projected to rise by about 130 won, with the tax rates for draught beer lifting to come in line with regular beer. This will see the tax burden for draught beer increase by 177,140 won per kilolitre. 

The burden on Korea's bars

When education tax and value-added tax is taken into account, the tax burden at the shipment stage is expected to soar by more than 200,000 won per kilolitre. Converted to a single 20-litre keg of draught beer used by ordinary establishments, the tax adds about 5,000 won more, translating to around 130 won per 500ml glass for consumers. While this may not seem like much per glass, the accumulated amount can grow significantly for larger venues with high sales volumes. Korea’s hospitality sector, which is already grappling with surging costs of labour, rent and raw materials, is  worried that the draught beer price hikes will lead to higher costs for the consumer. 

Venues close as Koreans cut back on booze

Over the past eight years, nearly half of Korea’s pubs have shut for good. Figures released by the National Tax Service (NTS) show that the number of casual pubs and beer houses nationwide fell to 28,178 in March 2026, down from 52,302 when records were first compiled in 2018. The decline means more than 24,000 establishments have disappeared, representing a 46% contraction in the sector. Casual pubs, known locally as ganee jujeom, recorded a 10.2% annual decline, falling from 8,894 to 7,985 businesses. Beer-focused establishments, or hof pubs, dropped by 9.4% over the same period, from 22,282 to 20,193.  Years of elevated inflation have increased rents, labour expenses and operating costs, placing pressure on small independent businesses that dominate South Korea’s pub sector. At the same time, traditional after-work drinking gatherings which were once a staple of corporate culture, have become less common, with consumers drinking less across the board.  The proof is in the numbers, with South Korea’s household alcohol spend seeing its sharpest drop in seven years in the first quarter of 2026. Traditionally, quarters containing the Lunar New Year or Chuseok holidays have seen alcohol purchases surge, but even these periods have now seen sales slip as alcohol sales dry up.

A regional picture

This is reflective of a broader regional trend, as consumers cut back on alcohol across the Asia Pacific region. Last year, three in 10 APAC consumers said they were drinking less alcohol in 2025 versus the prior year, according to data from NielsenIQ.  “APAC consumers are no longer drinking out of habit — they’re drinking with purpose,” James Phillips, head of beverage alcohol APAC at NielsenIQ, previously told the drinks business. He added: “The shift toward mindful consumption is not a passing trend, but a cultural reset that’s redefining how, when and why people drink. The key question – is this the new normal in the on-premise?  “If so, it presents big challenges for suppliers, manufacturers and operators, including the need to cater for moderating guests without alienating core consumers.  “Brands that can gain a deep understanding of this complex recalibration and adapt nimbly will be the ones that stay relevant in the months and years ahead.”

title: Why Woodforde’s has chosen to ‘celebrate the brewery’s Norfolk roots’
summary:
Woodforde’s Brewery has revealed new keg branding to match the business’s established cask presence in pubs and bars. But there is one extra reminder for its customers - Norfolk is where you can find great beer. Jessica Mason reports.

The post Why Woodforde’s has chosen to ‘celebrate the brewery’s Norfolk roots’ appeared first on The Drinks Business.
content:
Woodforde’s Brewery has revealed new keg branding to match the business’s established cask presence in pubs and bars. But there is one extra reminder for its customers - Norfolk is where you can find great beer. Jessica Mason reports. The Broadland-based brewery’s new look was applied across its entire keg range from  Norfolk Day (27 July) and included on keg lenses and glassware for pubs stocking its beers. As part of the rebrand, Woodforde’s will see its English Lager renamed as Woodforde’s Lager and Volt 0.5 will be named Woodforde’s 0.5 and, according to the company, the change celebrates the brewery’s Norfolk roots, with nods to local landmarks such as Norwich Cathedral, natural beauty spots and the famous Wherry boats which gave their name to Woodforde’s first ever beer. The beer sector is also in agreement in unison that Norfolk and specifically Norwich, is synonymous with historic beer and pub landmarks that are admired all over the world.

'Beautiful' and 'walkable'

Speaking to the drinks business, Woodforde’s CEO Paul Sullivan said: "Rewind to the days before Woodforde's formation in 1981 and Norfolk had lost its reputation for great beer, as national giants bought out and closed the county's breweries, starving local people of a pint they could be proud of. That's why Woodforde's was born." Sullivan explained to db that "Norfolk and its fields are home to world-famous malts, helping our beers stand out among the crowd as a real crowd pleaser. It's also home to some of the country's oldest and best pubs, something we should all be fiercely proud of." Describing Norwich, Varvar Brewery spokesperson, beer judge and Ukraine's first certified cicerone, Lana Svitankova also told db: "I don't know any other city having a pub where you can get a dark mild 10 out of 10 visits. All in all, it's beautiful, it's walkable, and the number of excellent places offering both cask and modern beer is plenty." Sullivan, said: “These simple yet captivating designs will fit in seamlessly with the competitors on the bar – they stand out for all the right reasons. We remain committed to our cask roots and our multi-award-winning range of traditional ales, but it was about time we brought our keg products into a uniform range.” World Beer Awards judge Mick Dore told db: "Norwich is one of Britain's finest beer cities. Built on beer, defined by its regional brews, where beer belongs and brewing leads."

Connecting with customers looking for quality

Sullivan explained that the Woodforde’s “name is synonymous with quality – and this new look with our name proudly at the centre will only create further trust and connection with customers looking for a quality pint, whether that’s cask, keg, bottle or can”. The relaunch follows the brewery having released its latest foray into the pale ale market, Woodforde’s Pale Ale, at this year’s Royal Norfolk Show. The 4% vegan and gluten free beer was also brewed as a celebration of Nelson’s County and proved a hit at this year’s show – with customers queuing at the bar to get their hands on the first pints.

Perfectly capturing Norfolk's splendour

Woodforde’s Pale Ale, alongside other beers in the brewery’s extensive range of keg products, will be served in the new-look glasses, while its range of canned beers will also feature Norfolk-themed artwork. Sullivan admitted: “We’ve listened to what our customers want – they don’t just want us to be the Taste of Norfolk, they want us to champion our magnificent home county and bask in the glory of our beautiful Broadland home. It has been a joy working alongside local illustrator Owen Mathers on the designs who has perfectly captured the splendour of our beautiful county – they would certainly make me want to visit. Every keg lens and glass shows exactly who we are – a brewery proud of our heritage serving up quality beer.” He added: "That's what we're all about here at Woodforde's – being the Taste of Norfolk. We champion local ingredients and the producers behind them – and our new keg branding ensures that message of love for all things Norfolk is at the forefront." Pubs looking to stock Woodforde’s keg range can contact the brewery.

title: Chateau Denmark Hill: “We’re hoping for 22 bottles this year, but we’re not allowed to sell it.”
summary:
Following the news that south London train station Denmark Hill is producing its first vintage of Bacchus, Sarah Neish speaks to the project's winemakers about staying on track and not going loco in the British heatwave.

The post Chateau Denmark Hill: “We’re hoping for 22 bottles this year, but we’re not allowed to sell it.” appeared first on The Drinks Business.
content:
Following the news that south London train station Denmark Hill is producing its first vintage of Bacchus, Sarah Neish speaks to the project's winemakers about staying on track and not going loco in the British heatwave.   As db reported yesterday, the UK's first railway station wine is well underway with the inaugural vintage from 'Chateau Denmark Hill' expected to be ready to drink next year. We caught up Nick Mair, co-winemaker for the south London project alongside Tony Coleman, to find out the triumphs and tribulations of growing vines just metres away from the train tracks. According to Nair, vibrations from trains passing at speed are "not an issue". "The vineyard is well above the tracks," he said. "Had it been at the same level we would have been more worried. The vines appear to be flourishing and rose bushes at the ends of each row bloom prodigiously. Plus, the prevailing wind is south westerly which then tends to run east along the tracks."

Winning formula

Intriguingly, neither Mair, nor Coleman, have had a career in wine, "though we are keen wine drinkers", Mair tells db. Rather, Coleman works in construction while Mair is a French and Spanish language teacher. The combination has proved to be a winning formula. "I tend to have ideas but Tony has the perseverance and construction background, without which the vineyard wouldn’t have happened," said Mair. That vineyard comprises 30 vines of aromatic white grape variety Bacchus, located within Denmark Hill train station's grounds in Camberwell. After Network Rail granted a special Community License to the Camberwell Society, of which Mair and Coleman are members, efforts were made to "clean up" the station and surrounding area. In Mair's words, the station "was one of the dodgier parts of Camberwell - a reputation we wanted to change. It was strewn with litter and we wanted to make it somewhere special." Along with installing various artworks and gardening projects, including a mini lavender farm, the Bacchus vines were planted as a way of helping the local community and commuters  to"engage more positively with the station," said Nair. It's all part of what he calls "the Provencification of Camberwell."

Forgiving variety

Bacchus was chosen by the novice winegrowers because Nair and Coleman, running point on the project, had noted that the variety was "successfully widely grown in South East England", and perhaps most importantly, is "forgiving for beginners!" However, before leaping straight in, the pair started off with another crop entirely. "I planted sunflowers in 2022 just to check [the soil's viability]," said Nair. "The horizon is very low and the vineyard is due south. We also checked soil records with Network Rail. Encouraged by a bumper sunflower crop, we removed bindweed in the autumn of 2023, terraced the ground and then augured in vertical posts, which was very hard work as we had no electricity or mechanical agricultural equipment." Thankfully, this is where Coleman's background in construction came into its own, meaning "we were able to make accurate plans to ensure an appropriate build, dig and structure" for the vineyard site. It hasn't all been sunshine and roses (or indeed sunflowers), with manpower a continual issue, especially for tending the vines.  At the start, Nair said, "we asked for volunteers who were prepared to help with the hard labour — we were honest about the scale of the project — and plenty wanted to dig in the vines, but nothing else."

New skills

While the team was short on professional winemaking experience, Nair had plenty of travel to winemaking regions under his belt, where he had picked up a thing or two. "As a French and Spanish teacher, I have spent some years in those countries," he said, adding that "part of the  A-level syllabus also used to allow for the study of a region – and 15 years of school trips to Jerez, including research interviews" not only helped him to "appreciate a good fino Sherry" but also to learn about the making and bottling of wines. He also spent a year in Cahors in the south of France, and time in the Alpes-Maritimes. Meanwhile, Coleman embarked on a vine-tending course at The Mount Vineyard in Shoreham, Kent, where he made the call to prune the Denmark Hill vines using the double Guyot method. According to Nair, "2026 will be the station's first proper harvest and the grapes are looking good - though a little rain at some stage would be helpful!" He of course refers to the unprecedented British summer heatwave, where the temperature has scarcely dipped below 30°C for months. Regarding the expected yield he revealed that the pair have pruned back to "something like nine bunches per vine" and given that the pair are beginners "we would be happy with 22 bottles in a first year – so a bottle per vine."

Not for sale

As the Camberwell Society "has an understanding with Network Rail that we will not sell any wine," interested parties will sadly not be able to purchase a bottle of Chateau Denmark Hill. At least for the timebeing. "It's really a passion project," said Nair, who has received advice, support and encouragement from various parties. "We have found it to be a very welcoming community, from growers to Masters of Wines, and independent local wine shops." "Given the excellence of English winemaking we are clearly enthusiasts rather than experienced viticulturists," he said. "Sip it and see will be our approach!" Are there plans to scale up the vineyard in the future? "There's not much available land in Camberwell," Nair quipped. However, when one is bitten by the winemaking bug, one tends to find a way, and the pair's next project might just take them further off the beaten tracks...

title: Campari profits fall despite stronger outlook for 2026
summary:
Davide Campari-Milano reported lower first-half profits despite delivering organic sales growth and improving earnings. The spirits group also upgraded its full-year margin outlook, citing a more favourable tariff environment and continued progress in streamlining its portfolio.

The post Campari profits fall despite stronger outlook for 2026 appeared first on The Drinks Business.
content:
Davide Campari-Milano reported lower first-half profits despite delivering organic sales growth and improving earnings. The spirits group also upgraded its full-year margin outlook, citing a more favourable tariff environment and continued progress in streamlining its portfolio. Davide Campari-Milano, the parent company of Campari and Aperol, saw its first-half 2026 profits decline, although its overall results were encouraging. Net profit for the period was €129 million, down from €206 million in the first six months of 2025. Net sales fell by 1.0% on a reported basis to €1.51 billion from €1.53 billion in 2025, reflecting the effect of portfolio disposals and foreign exchange movements. On an organic basis, net sales increased by 2.7%. Adjusted pre-tax earnings rose by 1.8% on a reported basis to €358 million from €352 million, while adjusted net profit increased by 4.7% to €226 million.

Tariff outlook improves

Looking ahead, the company raised its outlook for its full-year adjusted earnings margin due to what it believes is an improved tariff environment. The group now expects the full-year negative effect of tariffs to be €20 million, down from its previous forecast of €30 million.

Strategy gains momentum

Chief executive Simon Hunt said: "We are delivering on our strategy and growing with solid results in the first half of 2026 in terms of organic topline, profitability and a solid balance sheet. "At the same time, we are growing and gaining share across all our key markets, driven by our priority brands. "Our strategy of fewer bigger bets, including the disposal of non-priority brands, innovation and geographic expansion, is gaining traction while we continue to drive efficiency across each line of the P&L."

Portfolio reshaping continues

As part of its brand disposal programme, Campari is selling Bisquit & Dubouché Cognac and Cabo Wabo tequila to Cobblestone Brands, alongside a separate agreement to sell the Caribbean rum business of Bellonnie et Bourdillon Successeurs to a French private industry player.

title: Semaglutide cuts heavy drinking days in small alcohol trial
summary:
Semaglutide, the active ingredient in the in-demand diabetes drug Ozempic, reduced heavy drinking days and alcohol-related harm in a phase 2 clinical trial of people with alcohol use disorder.

The post Semaglutide cuts heavy drinking days in small alcohol trial appeared first on The Drinks Business.
content:
Semaglutide, the active ingredient in the in-demand diabetes drug Ozempic, reduced heavy drinking days and alcohol-related harm in a phase 2 clinical trial of people with alcohol use disorder. An oral form of semaglutide significantly reduced heavy drinking days among adults seeking treatment for alcohol use disorder, although it did not meet the study’s primary endpoint for laboratory-assessed craving. Researchers said the mixed results support larger trials rather than establishing the drug as a treatment. An oral form of semaglutide reduced heavy drinking days, alcohol-related harm and everyday cravings in a small clinical trial involving people with moderate to severe alcohol use disorder. The phase 2 study, published in the American Journal of Psychiatry, enrolled 50 treatment-seeking adults and compared daily oral semaglutide with a placebo over eight weeks. Participants received 3mg of semaglutide each day for four weeks, followed by 7mg daily for the remaining four weeks. The researchers found that semaglutide significantly reduced the number of heavy drinking days compared with placebo. Participants taking the drug also consumed fewer drinks on the days when they drank. However, semaglutide did not significantly reduce the study’s primary outcome, alcohol craving measured in a laboratory after participants were exposed to their preferred drink. It also failed to produce a statistically significant reduction in the average number of drinks consumed per calendar day.

Fewer heavy drinking days

During the final four weeks of treatment, participants receiving semaglutide recorded significantly fewer heavy drinking days than those taking the placebo. The drug also reduced drinks per drinking day, naturalistic alcohol cravings reported outside the laboratory and alcohol-related negative consequences. More people in the semaglutide group reduced their World Health Organisation risk drinking level by at least one category. Cannabis use days also declined among the small group of participants who reported using cannabis before the study, although this was an exploratory finding rather than one of the trial’s principal outcomes. The authors concluded that the results support continued investigation of semaglutide as a possible treatment for alcohol use disorder.

Primary endpoint missed

Despite the reductions in several drinking measures, the trial did not find a significant difference between semaglutide and placebo in cue-induced craving at week six. Participants were asked to hold and smell their preferred alcoholic drink for three minutes before rating the strength of their craving. The scores did not differ significantly between the two groups. The researchers also found no statistically significant reduction in drinks per calendar day during the final four weeks, although the result approached the study’s significance threshold. The findings therefore present a more qualified picture than reports suggesting GLP-1 medicines simply remove the desire to drink.

Early evidence

Interest in drugs such as semaglutide has grown following anecdotal reports from patients using GLP-1 receptor agonists for diabetes or weight management who said their interest in alcohol had diminished. Animal studies and observational research have also suggested that the medicines may influence reward pathways involved in alcohol consumption. A previous trial of injectable semaglutide involving people with less severe alcohol use disorder who were not seeking treatment found reductions in heavy drinking days, drinks per drinking day and craving. The latest trial tested an oral formulation among people actively seeking help and experiencing more severe alcohol problems. Researchers said oral treatment may prove attractive to patients who would prefer a tablet to a weekly injection.

Small trial requires caution

The study was conducted at a single US academic centre between November 2023 and October 2025 and included only 50 participants, all of whom had a body mass index of at least 25. Of those enrolled, 47 completed the eight-week treatment period. Three participants withdrew from the semaglutide group, including one who experienced an allergic reaction considered probably related to the medication. The authors acknowledged the trial’s moderate sample size and exploratory nature. No adjustment was made for testing multiple secondary outcomes, which means some positive findings require confirmation in larger studies. Semaglutide is not currently approved as a treatment for alcohol use disorder. The US Food and Drug Administration has approved three medications for the condition, which the researchers described as only modestly effective.

title: Lap of luxury: what’s the future for fine wine in China?
summary:
If China is to succeed on the fine wine stage, it will need not only high quality, but also all the trappings to attract a well-heeled audience, reports Amelie Maurice-Jones.

The post Lap of luxury: what’s the future for fine wine in China? appeared first on The Drinks Business.
content:
If China is to succeed on the fine wine stage, it will need not only high quality, but all the trappings to attract a well-heeled audience, reports Amelie Maurice-Jones. Chinese caviar has captivated global palates, while foie gras from the country increasingly finds itself on restaurant menus, as China outpaces France as the world’s largest producer of the canard delicacy. In more ways than one, China has all its ducks in a row, rising rapidly like a mighty fire horse as a powerhouse consumer and creator of luxury goods. Its wine is no exception. Flashback 20 years: Chinese winemaking boiled down to bulk-made, heavy-handed reds, while France commanded from its fine wine throne. Today, however, China is building a fine wine reputation of its own. With LVMH planting at 2,600 metres in Yunnan, and Ningxia family estates beating Bordeaux in international competitions, winemakers across China are redefining what it means to make luxury wine. The movement is politically backed too. After visiting Ningxia in 2020, President Xi Jinping pledged that the country’s wine would soon become “a marvel of the world”. But to win the world, you must first woo your home nation. To do so, Chinese producers aren’t simply borrowing the language of European luxury, but are, according to Anabelle Hourriez, chief growth officer at Shanghai-based branding agency Labbrand, “reinterpreting codes altogether – turning the bottle into a platform to celebrate China’s heritage, art and history”, in order to capture the interest of young, affluent consumers. 国潮Guochao (‘China Chic’) is no longer a fad, but a proud selling point, as Bordeaux’s magic spell wears off. Once upon a time, Shaun Rein, founder of the China Market Research Group and author of The End of Cheap China, supped with Chinese billionaires who’d opt for whatever the most expensive French red on the list was, regardless of quality. But today, “when you go to a banquet, serving a Chinese rather than French wine is considered cool and patriotic, showing support for the country, especially during a tough time geopolitically”, he explains. Hourriez makes no bones about it: “Consumers are no longer won over by French heritage.” As Chinese wine imports weaken, falling by 10.6% in the first quarter of 2026, according to customs data, opportunities open for Chinese wineries crafting a new definition of luxury wine.

Defining luxury in China

While high-end Western wine relies on centuries-old tradition, China’s relationship with the category is far younger. “That changes what luxury means,” explains Hourriez. “Alongside the traditional connoisseurs seeking authenticity and expertise, we’re seeing a distinctly Chinese consumer group emerge – cultural explorers, often first adopters, drawn as much to novelty and a story to tell as to the wine itself. That appetite for discovery is arguably sharper in China precisely because there’s no multi-generational wine culture to conform to.” This is echoed by Steven Gao, business director at Shanghai-based brand consultancy Landor. “Today, consumers are increasingly looking for brands with a story that belongs to China, rather than one borrowed from elsewhere,” he contends. This starts with appearances. When served at a professional dinner, the theatrical bottle-pouring moment creates fanfare before the first sip. “Packaging is the brand’s mianzi 面子– its face,” Gao explains, reflecting “not only the brand, but the person presenting it”. Due to this, “its design needs to carry social confidence. It must feel appropriate, considered and worthy of being seen in public”. Colour is crucial. Red and gold command prosperity and status – hence their heavy use in limited-edition Chinese New Year products. But, increasingly, Gao is noticing more muted tones – think celadon blue, ink grey, burnt ochre and deep wood – being used. He thinks these communicate “depth, provenance and confidence”. Typography can also express both origin and craft. “There is real potential in the tension between bespoke Chinese calligraphy and elegant Latin letter forms,” according to Gao. “A human, hand-drawn quality can signal founder vision and dedication, but it must be carefully controlled to avoid becoming a decorative cliché.” Hourriez continues: “A growing sophistication in typography treatment of Chinese characters can evoke a brand’s whole universe at a glance.” Naming can carry the same weight. Penfolds’ Chinese name, 奔富(Ben Fu), is a rare case of a transliteration that also means something genuinely auspicious – “rushing towards wealth”. This is proof, for Hourriez, that “traditional codes of status still work”. Ningxia’s Helan Qingxue winery takes the opposite route: its name – 贺兰晴雪(Helan Qingxue) – referring to one of the region’s classical “eight scenic views”, is rooting this modern winery in centuries-old local culture. Personalisation is also key to consumer engagement and market differentiation. From eco-friendly jute to lightweight silk and plush velvet, the wine gift bag market in China is evolving rapidly. Custom-made wine labels are growing in popularity, with intricate designs and embossed elements, as well as hot foil stamping and ice bucket-proof materials, evoking a sense of sophistication and rarity. Qianxi Crafts in Hangzhou, for instance, specialises in embossed soft metal wine stickers and, as part of the Yuanshi “Vineyard Adoption” programme 源石酒庄葡萄园认植计划, consumers can design their own labels, creating gifts guaranteed to impress at a Lunar New Year celebration. Symbolism, meanwhile, should stay subtle, suggests Gao. The strongest work avoids literal dragons, phoenixes or Great Wall imagery in favour of abstract references to landscape, terroir, craft or philosophy. “The objective is not to declare luxury loudly,” he adds. “It is to encode it: to create a bottle that appears calm at first glance, but reveals greater meaning the closer one looks.”

A sense of place

Just as packaging can communicate craftsmanship, so can setting. Domestic tourism has rocketed in China, with the extended Chinese New Year holiday this year seeing domestic trips boom to 596 million, and spending surpassing CNY803 billion – a leap of nearly 20% from the year before. The surge in travel spending is no coincidence, with the government adding two more days of public holiday from 2025 to boost leisure spending. This is a golden chance for wineries, with data from Persistent Market Research spotlighting Ningxia in particular as a rapidly developing go-to destination for local wine tourists. “The most compelling projects use landscape, material and visitor journey to turn the discovery of a wine into an immersive experience that becomes the peak of the brand experience,” says Gao. “The vineyard, the people and the story come together in one memorable setting.” In this way, he says, tourism can become “social currency”. With more than 200 registered wineries, Ningxia sits at the forefront of China’s fine wine movement. Guests visiting the region can experience everything from high-end tastings to glamping and farm-to-table dining that pairs Marselan and Cabernet blends with regional lamb and beef Hui cuisine. Visitors may also pair winery experiences with hikes into the Helan Mountains, tours to the ancient Western Xia Imperial Tombs, or voyages down the yellow Sha Po Tou river on sheep skin rafts. Then, along China’s eastern seaboard, there’s the coastal city of Yantai, which has emerged as the country’s most established wine hub, with its 63 wineries jumping on the rapidly expanding wine tourism train. Longting Winery hosted the ‘If the Sea Breeze Comes’ exhibition, combining wine with contemporary ink paintings by artist Huang Dan, while Michelin-starred restaurant Canton 8 has opened a branch at Runaway Cow Winery, hosting events for Ferrari owners’ clubs and Land Rover brand activities, reinforcing the company’s premium positioning. Meanwhile, at Longdai Winery, a packed catalogue of music festivals, seminars and bespoke dinners goes beyond traditional vineyard tours. Then there’s State Guest Winery, which has built a five-star State Guest International Hotel and a four-star State Guest Hotel alongside its vineyard operations; Jun Ding, which boasts a golf course; and Anuo Winery, which organises the Qushangu Concert, and has built camping sites and a cricket pitch. “These activities go beyond traditional tasting experiences, transforming wineries into cultural and lifestyle destinations where one can taste, explore and even stay,” a Yantai Wine and Vine Bureau spokesperson tells the drinks business. “The Yantai region is expanding the perception of premium wine from the dining table to a broader range of lifestyle scenes – including travel, art, sports and social engagement.” Upon arrival, architecture also helps create that ‘wow’ factor. Whether it’s Runaway Cow Winery’s kooky, cow-horn modernist design, State Guest Winery’s Tang-style Chinese aesthetic, or Longting’s resort-esque ambiance between mountain and sea, the building itself serves as the most direct “visual language” of brand positioning. “Luxury is ultimately about how people feel – seen, understood and cared for,” says Christine Jia of Mahota Winery. Located Shandong province, the winery blends viticulture and tourism in its 166-hectare estate. Its parent company, Prime Group International, operates four golf clubs near Shanghai, so Mahota’s luxury customers are golfers who share an appreciation for quality and heritage. Hourriez offers two more examples of showstopper wineries: “Ningxia’s Xige Estate turns the winery itself into the destination: a striking, circle-shaped, stone-walled complex at the foot of the Helan Mountains with guest rooms, an organic restaurant and a library, turning the winery into the destination,” she says. On the other hand, LVMH’s Ao Yun, located in the Tibetan foothills of Yunnan’s Meili Snow Mountains, does the opposite. “Its barn-like buildings across four remote villages are deliberately unshowy, and the hours needed to reach them by road become part of the luxury story: inaccessibility itself as the hospitality statement,” Hourriez explains. Her words offer an insight into the slipperiness of what luxury really is: a delicate tightrope between distance and closeness; exclusivity and access. “The most successful brands make buyers feel included, while preserving the exclusivity that makes inclusion meaningful,” Gao contends. For today’s luxury client, a simple winery tour won’t cut it. “Affluent consumers want access, participation and a sense of insider status, whether through private harvest dinners or invitation-only communities,” he continues.

Media magnetism

A bonus is that gorgeous buildings look great on social media. With China’s wine consumer base increasingly veering younger, according to IWSR research, this is paramount. Posting on platforms like Douyin and Xiaohongshu, visitors become brand ambassadors. “A livestream host with a personal connection to a winery, like Tiansai Vineyards’ Zhu Lili and her 2.1m followers, carries more weight than a critic’s score,” says Hourriez. When it comes to high-end wines, China’s Gen Z are drinking differently to their parents. They’re moving away from tannic reds to lighter styles, with drinking becoming a mode of self-expression, rather than a business obligation or simple status marker. But when winemakers make a luxury brand, one thing matters more than anything else – a sense of exclusivity. In this way, aiming to define ‘luxury Chinese wine’ is almost a moot point, with the country’s wine regions crafting their identities from what sets them apart from one another. “Scarcity,” specifies Gao, “is about the irreplaceability of place.” Ao Yun’s high-altitude Yunnan vineyards and Silver Heights’ family-led, biodynamic approach in Ningxia create forms of luxury rooted in “terroir, difficulty and authenticity”, defined directly in how they are distinguished and different from each other. This is echoed with lyrical charm by Landor’s executive creative director, Jamie Gandee, who says: “The more exciting future and opportunity for making brands more valuable lies in drawing directly from what each distinct wine promises and its unique terroir: Himalayan mist, Ningxia stone, desert sand, clay, vines and night skies.” According to Beijing-based Master of Wine Dr Edward Ragg high-end Chinese wine is associated with specific wineries rather than regions, be that Shanxi’s Grace Vineyard, or Emma Gao’s Silver Heights. While he expects to see Shangri-La become increasingly important, its elevation and topography mean that it’s unlikely to expand that much. Despite this, Dr Ragg expects to see emerging fine brands here in addition to the likes of Ao Yun and XiaoLing. “On a quasiBurgundian model, I expect to see small-batch, artisanal wines develop in particular up to Yunnan and neighbouring Sichuan,” he adds. Exclusivity is at the heart of Château Changyu Moser XV’s philosophy: “We do not copy,” the producer’s brand manager Yu Song makes clear. The winery is located in the foothills of the Helan Mountains in Ningxia. The unique style of the wine is how it crafts its high-end character. “It’s based on something no-one else has in the world,” Song says. These are reportedly the smallest Cabernet Sauvignon berries in the world. A normal Cabernet berry weighs 1.5g, versus Ningxia’s 1g. “This gives a unique opportunity to grow very special bunches and transform them into unique wines,” Song explains.

Grapes and styles

Despite the the sheer geographical scale of the wine regions, some think that China’s scope to become a fine wine superpower is unified in one grape – Marselan. Michael Palij MW, who led a masterclass on China’s emerging terroirs in London earlier this year, thinks the grape, which first arrived in China’s Hebei Province at the start of the 21st century, could “become [like] Argentina’s Malbec, or Chile’s Carmenere”. This reflects comments from Domaine Franco-Chinois winemaker Zhao Desheng, who last year called Marselan a “superstar in China”. His Huaili-based winery planted 2.75 hectares of the grape in 2001, adding to evidence that it could become a selling point for the nation. What about white wine? Recent research by Geisenheim University placed dry whites at the top of trending styles into 2027 in China, flagging opportunities for local producers to premiumise. “Chardonnay has evolved significantly in China,” Dr Ragg says. “There is a conception, at least amongst advanced wine lovers, that fine Chinese wines may be white and are often new, oak-influenced expressions of Chardonnay.” Previously speaking to db, Palij stated: “High-quality Chardonnay is going to be from Yunnan now,” claiming that the region’s long, cool growing seasons are uniquely positioned to produce delicate pours. But there are plenty of winemakers innovating when it comes to grape varieties outside the hard-hitters. Château Changyu Moser XV reports that its Blanc de Noir Cabernet, China’s first white Cabernet and launched 10 years ago, has been a “true winner” both globally and domestically. Xi Chen, MD of Greater China at global branding agency Dragon Rouge, also discusses how producers are experimenting with niche varieties to catch the eye of younger generations and stand out from the crowd. While Pushang pushes Marselan, Xige champions Cabernet Gernischt, Changpu Saperavi and Silk Road Petit Verdot and Malbec. Whatever the grape of choice, there’s one thing Palij sees in winemakers across the board: “There’s a real hunger for knowledge,” he enthuses. “There’s no shortage of money and there’s no shortage of will.” Those are certainly staple ingredients in a recipe for entrepreneurial success. “In the next 10 years, I hope the rest of the world understands that Chinese winemakers are winning not because they’re cheap or because of state subsidies,” Palic adds. “They’re winning because they have great innovation, production techniques and amazing quality. They’re winning because they’re working harder.” With passion, deep pockets and unflappable work ethic in hand, what does winning look like for Chinese winemakers? No longer, says Hourriez, is the question: “How do we sell more wine here?” but rather: “What do we want this brand to represent?” Mahota’s Jia is the voice of the chorus when she says: “We believe that the future of Chinese luxury wine lies not in imitating Bordeaux or Napa, but in having the confidence to tell our own story. As we look ahead, we see an opportunity to redefine what ‘premium Chinese wine’ means, not as a copy of Western traditions, but as an expression of Eastern philosophy in a glass.” db

title: On the up: which fine wines have been gaining value this year?
summary:
As the fine wine market shows clear signs of bottoming out, some regions and producers are spearheading the recovery, piquing the interest of collectors.

The post On the up: which fine wines have been gaining value this year? appeared first on The Drinks Business.
content:
As the fine wine market shows clear signs of bottoming out, some regions and producers are spearheading the recovery, piquing the interest of collectors. Although Liv-ex’s key indices are stabilising, there is wide variation between performances of individual component wines. Some probably have further to fall; others appear to have found their floors and are now tracking gently upwards. For buyers looking for safer moments to capitalise on the current market, wines that have shown evidence of reaching their floors may be the right place to start. Which wines fall into this category?

Defining an upward trend

There are many wines that are now trading above their 2025 lows, but a consistent upward trend is rarer to find. Even if a market price rises, there may be little transactional data to validate its direction. Thus, we turn to trades to assess true market trends. For the following analysis, we considered only wines that traded at least twice quarterly, with traded value totalling at least £5,000. A volume-weighted, quarterly average of trade price was then taken for each quarter since Q2 2025 – the broader market stabilised in Q3, so floors were likely to be reached around this time. An upward trend was defined as three or four quarter-on-quarter increases in volume-weighted average trade price over the past year.

Bordeaux

Bordeaux comprised more of the top-performing wines than any other region, thanks in part to its general liquidity (high volume and Liv-ex’s most traded region). Mouton dominated here, with five vintages featured on the list: 2015, 2005, 2010, 2018 and 2008. The 2015 had the strongest performance over the entire period, but appears to have come to rest at its 2020 lows, the bulk of its upward movement taking place in late 2025. Lafite 2015 tells a slightly different story. While, like Mouton 2015, it is currently trading at its 2020 lows, there is less evidence of prices coming to rest. With consistent upward momentum and a tight spread, there is more evidence pointing to continued positive price performance.

Champagne

As with Bordeaux, Champagne’s relative liquidity has allowed for more of the region’s wines to be considered in this analysis. Nevertheless, the Liv-ex Champagne 50 does appear to have now found support on its long-term upward trend line – as we settle into recovery, it should be a region to watch. Some of the most impressive performances (defined upward trends) of the past year, however, have been for non-vintage Champagnes such as Pol Roger Brut Réserve and Jacques Selosse’s Initial.

Other regions

Few other wines fulfilled the criteria for this list – though there are likely others with newer or less consistently defined upward trends. Of the three identified, Opus One 2013 looks most interesting, its trade frequency increasing as prices rise. It is now trading above its Market Price at similar levels to its 2022 peak. Taking a longer-term view, recent trades broadly align with a sustained upward trend.

About Liv-ex

Liv-ex is the global exchange for fine wine, market data and insight. We enable wine businesses to trade smarter with trusted data, technology and logistics. Members access £100m-worth of wine, real-time pricing and 620+ partners worldwide – all with secure settlement and delivery built in. Learn more at www.liv-ex.com.

title: Global alcohol deaths fall 26% since 2010, new analysis finds
summary:
Alcohol-attributable deaths have fallen by around a quarter worldwide since 2010, according to a new analysis of Global Burden of Disease data. 

The post Global alcohol deaths fall 26% since 2010, new analysis finds appeared first on The Drinks Business.
content:
Alcohol-attributable deaths have fallen by around a quarter worldwide since 2010, according to a new analysis of Global Burden of Disease data.  A new analysis of global health data has found that alcohol-attributable mortality has fallen by approximately 26% since 2010, suggesting significant progress towards international targets to reduce alcohol-related harm. The report, published by the International Alliance for Responsible Drinking (IARD), analysed the latest figures from the Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation's Global Burden of Disease (GBD) study. Alongside the decline in alcohol-related deaths, the analysis found that age-standardised disability-adjusted life years (DALYs) linked to alcohol fell by around 23% over the same period. High alcohol use exposure, measured using the Global Burden of Disease Summary Exposure Value (SEV), declined by approximately 10%.

Progress towards 2030 target

The findings are measured against the 2010 baseline established when United Nations member states adopted the World Health Organisation's Global Strategy to Reduce the Harmful Use of Alcohol. Under that strategy, countries agreed to work towards reducing the harmful use of alcohol by 20% by 2030. According to IARD, the reported 26% reduction in alcohol-attributable mortality suggests substantial progress towards that objective. Julian Braithwaite, president and chief executive of IARD, said: "These findings are encouraging and show that meaningful reductions in alcohol-related harm are achievable. "But global averages mask significant differences between countries and regions, and continued progress cannot be taken for granted. Looking across mortality, disability and exposure together provides a stronger evidence base to help governments, healthcare providers and communities make more informed decisions, strengthen ongoing efforts and focus resources where they are most needed."

Multiple factors at play

The report does not attribute the improvement to any single intervention. Instead, IARD said the trend is likely to reflect the combined effects of changing drinking patterns, improvements in healthcare, public health initiatives and broader social and economic development. The analysis draws on estimates from the latest Global Burden of Disease study through 2024. IARD also noted that the Global Burden of Disease study and World Health Organisation produce separate estimates using different methodologies, meaning their figures should not be compared directly. Instead, the analysis is presented as a complementary assessment of long-term trends in alcohol-related harm. Debate over alcohol policy continues The findings arrive as debate continues over the most effective ways to reduce alcohol-related harm. As previously reported by the drinks business, the World Health Organisation argued in January that alcoholic drinks have become "too affordable" and called on governments to strengthen alcohol taxation. The UN health agency described higher alcohol taxes as one of the strongest public health measures available to reduce harmful consumption, alongside wider prevention strategies.

title: Rwanda shuts down 101 liquor production sites amid public health concerns
summary:
Rwanda’s government has ordered the closure of 101 alcoholic beverage manufacturing facilities and revoked their production licences as part of a broader crackdown on illicit alcohol.

The post Rwanda shuts down 101 liquor production sites amid public health concerns appeared first on The Drinks Business.
content:
Rwanda’s government has ordered the closure of 101 alcoholic beverage manufacturing facilities and revoked their production licences as part of a broader crackdown on illicit alcohol. On Monday (3 August), the Rwanda government’s Food and Drugs Authority (FDA) issued a announcement announcing the closure of 101 sites that produced alcoholic beverages The production facilities produce an array of alcoholic drinks including vodka, gin, flavoured wines and banana-based alcoholic beverages. The regulator also ordered the immediate removal of all advertising materials linked to the products and instructed manufacturers, distributors and retailers to withdraw them from the market and halt distribution.

Health and safety concerns The FDA warned that businesses failing to comply would face punitive measures and urged the public to stop consuming alcohol produced by the blacklisted facilities. Among the companies affected are Kasesa Distillers and Distributors Ltd, which produces African Gin, and Yego Manufacturers Ltd, maker of Leyon Vodka, Lion Heart Rum and Gorilla Gin.

The announcement came a day after the regulator ordered the closure of eight liquor manufacturers "in the interest of public health". Those companies included Ingufu Gin, NBG, Sky Drop Industries, Africana Buffalo, Nopa Company, Roots Investment Group, Rugal Agro-processing Company and Zhonglu Industrial Liability Company. The enforcement action follows growing concerns over the health impact of illicit alcohol in Rwanda. The Ministry of Health recently launched the "Tunywe Less" (translated to "Let's Drink Less") campaign after surveys pointed to rising alcohol consumption rates, particularly among young people.

Climbing drinking rates

According to the Rwanda Biomedical Centre's 2022 national survey on non-communicable disease risk factors, alcohol consumption rose from 41% of the population in 2013 to 48% in 2022. The latest Rwanda Demographic and Health Survey (RDHS-7), published by the National Institute of Statistics of Rwanda (NISR), found that 15% of men and 7% of women consume alcohol daily. Among adults aged 15 to 49, half of men and 36% of women reported drinking alcohol in the month before the survey. Speaking on Rwanda Television on Sunday, health minister Sabin Nsanzimana said more than 500 people had been treated this year for complications linked to illicit alcohol. He said around 50 people had died, while more than 100 had suffered vision loss.

title: Woman charged for selling fake alcohol mixed with tap water
summary:
A woman in Quảng Ngãi province in central Vietnam has been charged for producing bootleg spirits made by mixing industrial alcohol with tap water, before selling the counterfeit alcohol on to customers.

The post Woman charged for selling fake alcohol mixed with tap water appeared first on The Drinks Business.
content: A woman in Quảng Ngãi province in central Vietnam has been charged for producing bootleg spirits made by mixing industrial alcohol with tap water, before selling the counterfeit alcohol on to customers. Police in Quang Ngai Province said on Sunday that they had prosecuted Luu Thi Thuy, 52, from Kon Tum Ward, on charges of manufacturing and trading counterfeit food and drink, Vietnam Today has reported. The investigation is currently continuing, Quang Ngai Province Police said. According to the province's Economic Police Division, officers seized 103 plastic 30-litre containers containing cloudy, white liquid from Thuy's business premises. As part of the raid, officials also discovered nine containers of industrial alcohol and 80 containers holding more than 200 litres of finished liquor that had allegedly been prepared for sale. Police said Thuy admitted purchasing high-strength alcohol of unknown origin before mixing it with tap water to produce the resulting white liquor for sale. Authorities warned that liquor made from industrial alcohol or alcohol of unknown origin can lead to serious health risks, due to the potential that it could contain methanol, a toxic substance that can cause severe poisoning, blindness and death.

title: Beyoncé takes full control of SirDavis whisky after buying out Moët Hennessy
summary:
Beyoncé has taken full ownership of SirDavis American Whisky, ending Moët Hennessy's involvement less than two years after the brand's launch. The move comes as LVMH continues to reshape its drinks division following a prolonged downturn in Cognac and Champagne sales.

The post Beyoncé takes full control of SirDavis whisky after buying out Moët Hennessy appeared first on The Drinks Business.
content:
Beyoncé has taken full ownership of SirDavis American Whisky, ending Moët Hennessy's involvement less than two years after the brand's launch. The move comes as LVMH continues to reshape its drinks division following a prolonged downturn in Cognac and Champagne sales. Beyoncé has acquired full ownership of SirDavis American Whisky after buying out Moët Hennessy's stake in the brand she launched alongside the luxury drinks group in 2024. Financial terms of the transaction have not been disclosed. SirDavis marked Moët Hennessy's first spirits brand created from the ground up in the United States and represented the company's attempt to strengthen its position in the American whiskey market. The brand is named after Beyoncé's paternal great-grandfather, Davis Hogue, a farmer and moonshiner in the American South during Prohibition.

Moët Hennessy exits

The reasons behind Moët Hennessy's exit have not been disclosed, and neither party has commented publicly on the rationale for the change in ownership. SirDavis remains bottled at 44% ABV and is produced from a mash bill of 51% rye and 49% malted barley. The whiskey is distilled by MGP Ingredients before being finished, blended and bottled in Beyoncé's home state of Texas. The liquid was developed by Dr Bill Lumsden, director of whisky creation at Glenmorangie and Ardbeg, working alongside SirDavis head blender Cameron George and Beyoncé herself. Retailing at around US$89 (£79 in the UK), the whiskey was designed to combine classic American rye character with influences drawn from Scotch and Japanese whisky.

Strategic shift

The ownership change comes during a period of restructuring at Moët Hennessy, which has faced weaker demand for both Cognac and Champagne in key international markets. As previously reported by the drinks business, LVMH denied speculation last year that Diageo could sell its 34% stake in Moët Hennessy. More recently, the luxury group has introduced management changes across its wines and spirits division as it seeks to improve performance. Beyoncé's decision to take sole ownership gives the global artist complete control over the future direction of SirDavis as the premium American whiskey brand continues to establish itself in an increasingly competitive category.

From partnership to sole ownership

When SirDavis launched in August 2024, Beyoncé described the whiskey as a tribute to her family's history and her long-standing appreciation of the category. "I've always been drawn to the power and confidence I feel when drinking quality whisky and wanted to invite more people to experience that feeling," she said at the time.

title: Friarwood Wine & Spirits closes after 59 years, as it enters administration
summary:
London independent merchant Friarwood Fine Wines and Spirits, which has been trading for nearly six decades, has been placed into administration.

The post Friarwood Wine & Spirits closes after 59 years, as it enters administration appeared first on The Drinks Business.
content: London independent merchant Friarwood Fine Wines and Spirits, which has been trading for nearly six decades, has been placed into administration. According to documents filed at Companies House on 20 July, the company went into administration on 3 July, with William Antony Batty and Hugh Francis Jesseman from Antony Batty & Company Ltd appointed as administrators. Its website shared the news that it would soon be closing the business and thanked its customers for their loyalty and support "over the years". Although the store is now closed, its website assures customers that it would continue to ship orders already placed, with collection available from its Parsons Green store until the end of this week (7 August). The business was founded in 1967 by Peter Bowen as a London-based wholesaler, only later branching into retail from its Parsons Green office in 2001. On Bowen's death in 2014, his widow offered to sell the business to Canadian-born Ben Carfagnini, who had started as an intern with Bowen as his mentor.  He took over the business in February 2015, refreshing the branding and bringing a younger management team on board. He also developed a greater tech-focus - under Bowen, the merchant’s Parson’s Green shop had operated sales and stock solely using pen and ink, with neither E-pos or Wifi on site - as well as expanding the range which had been heavily Bordeaux and Burgundy-centric to embrace the Loire, Rhone and Bulgaria, as well as Italy, Australia, Argentina, Chile and Canada. Under Carfagnini, the business rolled out its first e-commerce venture in 2016 and opened a second retail outlet on the High Street of Wimbledon Village in 2017, the combined retail operation contributing about a third of the overall business at the time, with the balance focusing on its wholesale business. This sold wines into hotels, restaurants and private members clubs, focusing on  offering wines "that can’t be found anywhere else in London", with the majority coming direct from producers. It later expanded into premium spirits in 2023.  Although the company does not publish its profits and losses and applies for a small business exemption, its most recent financial records showed that in the year to 31 March 2025, its debts rose from £1.79million to £2.22million, while its asset more than halved, falling from £675,491 in 2024 to £319,352.

title: More than £374 million wiped off Endeavour Group profits
summary:
Endeavour’s profits are expected to plummet from AU$426m in 2025 to just AU$52m in 2026. The dramatic slide reflects last week's announcement that the group is offloading most of its Australian wineries in a bid to slash its grape growing by 80%.

The post More than £374 million wiped off Endeavour Group profits appeared first on The Drinks Business.
content:
Endeavour’s profits are expected to plummet from AU$426m in 2025 to just AU$52m in 2026.
